thread.title: IBM: A Long Work-In-Progress - International Business Machines Corporation (NYSE:IBM)

author: ALT Perspective
title: IBM: A Long Work-In-Progress - International Business Machines Corporation (NYSE:IBM)

organizations.name: long work-in-progress - international business machines corporation

text:
IBM's Share Price Has Much Catching Up To Do It has been nine months since my initial article on IBM ( IBM ) where I laid out the two key reasons why I believed Berkshire Hathaway (NYSE: BRK.A )(NYSE: BRK.B ) would "sell its remaining IBM stake entirely or at least a substantial portion of its holding". The comments following the article were generally of the point that IBM (and its share price) was probably on the verge of a turnaround, that Warren Buffett could even be building his IBM stake against what he was publicly implying, and positive tailwinds such as the corporate tax cut could offset the weakness at the legacy businesses while its cloud services and blockchain endeavors step up to the fore. The fact as we all know by now is that Berkshire Hathaway sold nearly 95 percent of its IBM stake by the end of last year. According to what Buffett had revealed during an interview with CNBC, Berkshire Hathaway has also cleared the remaining two million shares.
What intrigued me to revisit IBM was the eye-catching news that IBM has now a supercomputer that has "leapt ahead" of a Chinese rival which had held the title of the "world's fastest" for two years. What's even more exciting is the fact that this isn't just a mere edging out in speed for the sake of recapturing the title. The newly introduced supercomputer by IBM dubbed Summit is reportedly nearly twice as fast as the peak speed for Chinese supercomputer Sunway TaihuLight.
I decided to check out the stock price movement and not surprisingly, it was up the day of the announcement on June 8, albeit just a small bump. Over the past one year, IBM is down 5 percent, while the S&P 500 ( SPY ) is up around 15 percent. The technology sector as exemplified by the Technology Select Sector SPDR ETF ( XLK ) is up 30 percent, close to Apple's ( AAPL ) gain of 32 percent. Over a longer period, the difference is even more stark. Clearly, IBM has much catching up to do for its shareholders.
IBM data by YCharts The Slide In Margins IBM plunged around 8 percent the next trading day despite posting its 2018 first-quarter results which beat on both EPS and revenue. The cloud revenue was also impressive, rising 20 percent to $17.7 billion, against the overall company-level revenue gain of 10 percent (constant currency). However, the market was sorely disappointed that its margins missed analysts' consensus estimates. A poorer than expected guidance also dampened sentiments.
Over the past three years, IBM has seen its gross profit margin decline from around 50 percent to the current 46 percent on a trailing-twelve-month ("TTM") basis. This has a more profound impact as we move lower the income statement. For instance, the net profit margin has whittled by half to 7.1 percent on a TTM basis by the last reported quarter.
IBM Gross Profit Margin (TTM) data by YCharts The company executives blamed certain one-off items which negatively impacted the margins in Q1 2018 but as seen from the chart above, the margin slide is not a one-two quarter phenomenon. To mitigate the margin erosion, Jim Kavanaugh, the SVP and CFO of IBM, said in the earnings call that the company has been seeking to improve its "workforce optimization productivity". That involved refining the company's "skill pyramid" and "infusing AI and automation to improve delivery". As a company outsider, it is not possible to fully appreciate how such initiatives can impact the margins and we really have to observe if the jargons do indeed translate into something tangible in the following quarterly results.
Workforce Downsizing At IBM One way to cut costs is by reducing the headcount, which IBM is adopting. After peaking in 2013, IBM's total employee count has reduced to 397,800 by the end of last year. The drop has been largely attributable to a combination of divestitures and layoffs. The current employee size is now back to pre-2010 levels. However, despite the smaller workforce, its revenue per employee continues to shrink and each employee now contributes around three-quarters of the revenue one did ten years ago. Net income per employee fell precipitously in 2017, halving to $142 thousands per employee. Apparently, the downsizing, while making for dramatic headlines, has not been sufficient to stem the dwindling contribution per head at IBM.
IBM Total Employees (Annual) data by YCharts Interestingly, I realized that IBM is not alone in this seemingly futile struggle against improving its revenue per employee. Its peers in technology such as Apple and Amazon ( AMZN ) similarly saw their revenue per employee shrink over the past years. Even companies like Alphabet ( GOOG )( GOOGL ), the holding company for search engine giant Google and streaming website YouTube, which has seen improving revenue per employee over the same period, the pace of increase has lagged behind its employee addition growth rate. Hence, while it is imperative that IBM rationalize its workforce periodically to streamline its operations following a series of acquisitions and divestitures, more needs to be done if it wishes to improve its productivity metrics.
IBM Total Employees (Annual) data by YCharts Investor Takeaway Early in the year, I wrote about the setback IBM faced in China with regards to its cloud ambition in the fast-growing country. IBM appears to have moved on from having bad news dominate the market attention on its name. Despite its laggard performance, analysts are apparently warming up to IBM as a recovery candidate. IBM's price targets have been raised over the past year. Currently, the price upside based on the consensus is around 15 percent, among the meatiest it has been over the past one year. The good news for investors is that the "impending sale by Berkshire Hathaway" overhang is now gone and the business weakness should have long been priced-in.
IBM Price Target data by YCharts Nonetheless, looking from the technical charting perspective, IBM's share price appears to be trapped in a descending triangle formation which is a bearish chart pattern setup. Keen investors might wish to wait for a breakout from the resistance line before taking a larger position in the stock.
What's your take? Do you see a sustained business recovery and consequently a share price rebound in IBM? If so, do you think it can break out of the descending triangle chart pattern? Please freely share your thoughts, let me know if you found this article useful or provide your feedback in the comments section.
